tldr: Even state-of-the-art VLA models that achieve near 100% success on standard benchmarks suffer a performance drop of over 50% once an unexpected failure occurs. This paper introduces LIBERO-Recover, a benchmark designed to evaluate and train recovery capabilities from naturally occurring execution failures.
hero_caption: Overview of LIBERO-Recover. Natural failure scenes caused during task execution by SOTA VLA and WAM models are collected and structured into 4 recovery levels and 16 evaluation axes. As shown in the top-right radar chart, even top-tier models still face severe challenges in recovering from failure.
overview:
Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World Action Models (WAMs) are remarkable, reaching nearly 100% success rates on the standard benchmark LIBERO. However, taking these numbers at face value to conclude that models are ready for real-world deployment is premature.

Existing evaluations focus almost entirely on one-shot success starting from pristine initial states. In real-world robot operation, failures like slipped grasps, collisions, and unintended object displacements inevitably occur. A truly reliable robot needs more than just the ability to complete tasks under ideal conditions; it must recognize failures, restore disturbed states, and resume the task.

To bridge this gap, the authors built LIBERO-Recover, a large-scale benchmark rooted in naturally occurring failures during actual model execution rather than artificial environmental perturbations. They constructed over 2,000 recovery scenarios from SOTA model failure behaviors, classified them into four recovery levels, and collected human teleoperated recovery trajectories.

Evaluating six representative models revealed that, despite high scores on standard benchmarks, their performance plummeted by more than 50% as soon as they encountered failures. While models can manage local trajectory adjustments, they struggle significantly with reasoning required to restore heavily disturbed objects or environments, uncovering a critical blind spot for real-world deployment.
contributions: Demonstrated that relying solely on task success rates from ideal initial states creates a critical blind spot, proving that evaluating failure recovery is essential for robot robustness.
Constructed LIBERO-Recover, a natural failure recovery benchmark consisting of 4 recovery levels, 130 subtasks, and 16 evaluation axes extracted from the models' own execution errors.
Collected 3,184 high-quality human teleoperated recovery trajectories and introduced dedicated evaluation metrics such as Recovery Success Rate (RSR).
Extensively evaluated state-of-the-art VLA and WAM models, revealing a substantial gap between standard task success rates and failure recovery capabilities.

sections.heading: The trap behind 100% success rates: Are robots truly smart?
sections.summary: Existing benchmarks fail to measure true model robustness by prioritizing one-shot task completion from pristine states. This section explains the motivation and overview of LIBERO-Recover, introduced to evaluate the failure recovery capability crucial for real-world deployment.
sections.details:
State-of-the-art VLA and WAM models consistently achieve near 100% success rates on standard benchmarks like LIBERO. Scores are so high that some recent papers even omit LIBERO, claiming it is too easy to differentiate models. However, this creates a major pitfall.

Conventional benchmarks evaluate only whether a model can complete a task in a single attempt starting from predefined, well-arranged initial states. But in real-world manipulation, irreversible failures such as dropping an object or colliding and knocking things out of place inevitably happen. A truly practical robot must recognize failures, restore the disturbed state, and resume the task.

Recently, robustness benchmarks that randomly perturb environments have emerged, but they only test generalization against static environmental variations where humans modify object poses or textures in advance. No framework existed to evaluate dynamic failures caused mid-task by the robot itself and the subsequent recovery process.

To address this, the authors propose LIBERO-Recover, a benchmark built by collecting real execution failures from SOTA models. Evaluating across 130 subtasks revealed that existing models have remarkably low recovery capabilities, proving that high standard benchmark scores do not guarantee real-world reliability.

captions.F1: Overview of LIBERO-Recover. Natural failures are extracted from the execution logs of diverse VLA models and systematized into four recovery levels (from L1: Action Retry to L4: Environmental Recovery), accompanied by human demonstrations and detailed 16-dimensional capability evaluations.

sections.heading: The evolution of imitation learning and the neglected problem of handling failure
sections.summary: While robot policies have advanced dramatically with the rise of VLAs and WAMs, they remain focused on imitating successful trajectories. This section reviews the history of benchmarks and outlines why dedicated failure recovery evaluation has been missing.
sections.details:
### Advances in Robot Manipulation Policies
Robot manipulation has evolved from traditional visual imitation learning to VLAs (such as RT-1, OpenVLA, $\pi_0$, and GR00T) that integrate vision, language, and action using multimodal foundation models. More recently, WAMs (such as UniVLA and Cosmos-Policy) incorporate world models that predict future states conditioned on actions, enhancing long-term planning capabilities. However, these models primarily focus on accurately predicting and executing successful trajectories. Almost no work has systematically modeled recovery from unexpected failure states.

### Evolution and Limitations of Benchmarks
Simulation benchmarks began with RLBench and LIBERO, advancing through CALVIN, SimplerEnv, RoboCasa, and variants like LIBERO-Plus for perturbations and LIBERO-Safety for safety constraints. Yet, these test whether a task can be finished under human-defined distribution shifts (such as changes in object layout or appearance), rather than testing recovery from a disrupted state that occurred during execution. LIBERO-Recover fills this gap by grounding its evaluation in authentic, execution-derived failure logs.

sections.heading: How do you collect and categorize realistic failures?
sections.summary: The authors systematized 2,178 recovery scenarios generated from model execution errors into four difficulty levels (L1–L4) based on required reasoning depth. This section details the automated failure detection pipeline and the human recovery dataset collection.
sections.details:
### Problem Formulation and Definition of Failure
When a robot navigates from an initial state $s_0$ toward a goal $\mathcal{G}$, it may drift into an unexpected intermediate state $s_f$. A state where continuing the original action plan cannot achieve the goal, yet the goal remains reachable through appropriate corrective actions, is defined as a Recoverable Failure State. Unlike minor environmental noise, recovering from a failure state requires understanding what went wrong and generating a new recovery trajectory $\pi_{\mathrm{rec}}$.

### Four Levels of Recovery Difficulty
Four recovery levels were defined based on the depth of state reasoning required to recover:
- **$L_1$ Action Retry:** The target object's state is virtually unchanged, such as a missed grasp. Recovery requires simply re-attempting the grasp.
- **$L_2$ Action Adaptation:** The target object moved slightly due to an imperfect interaction. The robot must adapt its reach to the shifted position rather than repeating the exact same motion.
- **$L_3$ Object State Recovery:** The target object's pose was severely disrupted, such as a bowl being tipped over. The robot must restore the object's orientation or position before resuming the task.
- **$L_4$ Environmental Recovery:** Non-target surrounding objects were knocked over and now obstruct the task. The robot requires topological reasoning to clear task-irrelevant obstacles before continuing.

### Automated Construction Pipeline and Statistics
Instead of manually designing failure setups, the authors recorded execution videos of actual models (such as $\pi_0$, OpenVLA, and Cosmos-Policy). A large VLM (Qwen3.5-27B-Instruct) then identified the exact time window of the failure, allowing the exact physical state to be extracted from the simulator. The VLM also analyzed the post-failure consequences to assign difficulty levels (L1–L4). In total, 2,178 scenarios across 130 subtasks were generated. Additionally, 4 human experts used a SpaceMouse to collect 3,184 recovery trajectories across 413 scenarios.

captions.F3: Timeline examples across the four recovery levels (L1–L4) defined in LIBERO-Recover. Required reasoning depth increases progressively from simply retrying an action in L1, adapting to displacements in L2, uprighting a tipped object in L3, to clearing obstructing obstacles in L4.
captions.F4: Construction pipeline for LIBERO-Recover scenarios. Failure intervals (Pre, During, Post) are detected from model execution videos using Qwen3.5, and the exact simulator states are saved, enabling human recovery data collection and model fine-tuning.

sections.heading: How is recovery measured? Dedicated evaluation metrics
sections.summary: This section introduces the structure of the teleoperated expert demonstration dataset and three novel metrics (RSR, RD, and RC) designed to rigorously evaluate failure recovery performance.
sections.details:
### The LIBERO-Recover Dataset
To support model training for recovery, 4 skilled operators collected 3,184 recovery demonstrations using a SpaceMouse. The dataset covers 413 failure scenarios sampled evenly across five task suites.

### Three Dedicated Evaluation Metrics
To evaluate recovery from multiple angles, the following metrics were designed:
- **Recovery Success Rate (RSR):** The proportion of trials that successfully achieve the original task goal starting from a failure state. Both overall scores and level-specific scores $\mathrm{RSR}_{L_1} \sim \mathrm{RSR}_{L_4}$ are calculated.
- **Recovery Degradation (RD):** Quantifies how much task performance is degraded due to the failure. It measures the drop between pre-failure and post-failure performance as $1 - (M_{\mathrm{post}} + \epsilon)/(M_{\mathrm{pre}} + \epsilon)$; lower values indicate better preservation of capability.
- **Recovery Consistency (RC):** Evaluates how consistently a model recovers across diverse failure states within the same task. Defined using the standard deviation of success rates across tasks, values closer to 1 signify stable, uniform recovery performance.

sections.heading: Experimental findings: SOTA VLAs struggle, and hints for successful recovery
sections.summary: Evaluating representative models such as OpenVLA and $\pi_0$ uncovered a large gap between standard scores and recovery ability. Reducing action chunk size and providing temporal context proved effective for recovery.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup and Key Findings
Six models were evaluated: OpenVLA-OFT, $\pi_0$, $\pi_0$-Fast, GR00T-N1.5, Wan2-Policy, and Cosmos-Predict2-Policy. Key findings include:

- **Standard benchmark success is misleading:** Models boasting high scores in standard setups saw performance drop by more than 50% when encountering natural failures. For example, Wan2-Policy outperformed GR00T-N1.5 by +14.40% on standard LIBERO-100, but trailed by -5.0% on recovery evaluation, completely reversing their ranking.
- **Local adjustments succeed, but state restoration fails:** Across all models, success rates plummeted as difficulty rose. Models could manage L1/L2 reaching adjustments, but struggled heavily with L3/L4 tasks like uprighting a tipped bowl or removing obstacles, which demand deep reasoning about object geometry and spatial layout.
- **Failures snowball into catastrophic collapse:** Performance degraded severely during post-failure retries. Average model success dropped from 15.0% to 6.7% on LIBERO-Spatial, and collapsed from 26.2% to just 0.3% on LIBERO-100 (RD = 100%). Repeating actions without recovery competence compounds the damage.
- **World action models (WAMs) show higher stability:** WAM models like Cosmos and Wan2 achieved higher consistency metrics (RC of 0.8837 and 0.8698, respectively) than conventional VLAs. Explicitly modeling state transitions provides greater resilience to unexpected states.

### Recipes for Improving Recovery
- **Smaller action chunk size:** Reducing the chunk size from 32 to 4 markedly improved recovery success. High-frequency closed-loop control with frequent visual feedback is vital after failures.
- **Providing initial frame context:** Supplying the task's initial image as a visual prompt improved OpenVLA's recovery rate from 20.8% to 26.8%. Comparing the intended initial state with the current scene helps the model infer what broke.
- **Transfer gap of recovery data:** Fine-tuning on collected recovery trajectories boosted scores on the recovery benchmark itself, but contributed little to recovering from errors that occurred naturally during standard LIBERO execution. Teaching recovery policies alone is insufficient; models also need mechanisms to recognize their own failures online.

captions.F10: Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) visualization of training trajectories in LIBERO-Recover (left, red) versus standard LIBERO (right, blue). Standard trajectories disperse broadly across the workspace, whereas recovery data concentrates densely around critical interaction regions where contact and grasp failures frequently occur.

sections.heading: Toward robots that can recover from failure
sections.summary: This paper presents LIBERO-Recover, shifting robot evaluation from one-shot success to failure recovery. It opens a new direction toward truly robust embodied agents.
sections.details: This work introduces LIBERO-Recover, fundamentally shifting the evaluation paradigm of robot manipulation models from 'Can the robot succeed?' to 'Can the robot recover after failure?' Evaluations across realistic failure scenarios revealed that even top-performing models have severe limitations when recovery requires deep state reasoning.\n\nWhile high-frequency closed-loop control and temporal context referencing initial states improve recovery, a transfer gap remains: simply mixing in offline recovery data does not fully resolve spontaneous execution errors. LIBERO-Recover serves as a foundational benchmark toward building genuinely capable embodied intelligence that can autonomously bounce back from failures.

takeaways: Do not rely solely on standard benchmark scores: even models with near 100% success drop by over half upon experiencing a single execution failure.
Smaller action chunks improve failure recovery significantly by enabling frequent visual feedback in a tight closed loop.
Providing the initial state frame as visual context helps the model identify discrepancies with the disturbed state, substantially boosting recovery performance.
Imitation learning on static recovery trajectories alone fails to handle spontaneous errors during execution; developing online failure self-recognition is an essential next step.
limitations: Evaluations are currently limited to simulation (LIBERO); validating failure recovery on physical robots with complex real-world dynamics and sensor noise remains future work.
Collecting recovery demonstrations relies heavily on human teleoperation, pointing to the need for scalable and autonomous failure collection and recovery data generation methods.
Detecting failure intervals and annotating difficulty levels relies on VLM (Qwen3.5) reasoning, meaning potential biases and inaccuracies from automated annotation cannot be entirely ruled out.
